title: The Blue Carbuncle: A Sherlock Holmes Case
author: Arthur Conan Doyle
retoldBy: Retold for Grammar Stream from “The Adventure of the Blue Carbuncle” by Arthur Conan Doyle (1892)
blurb: Cases for Young Detectives. At Christmas, a battered old hat and a fat goose are found in a London street, and inside the goose is a stolen jewel. Sherlock Holmes follows the trail of the goose across frosty London to catch the real thief.
note: A retelling for young readers that keeps Doyle’s plot, clues and deductions. Changes: Holmes’s guess that Henry Baker drinks is left out and the remark about his wife is softened; brandy becomes a glass of water and the beer at the inn is dropped; the jewel’s violent history is trimmed. Short explanations (a commissionaire, a goose’s crop) and “Clue check” questions are added.

chapters.title: Chapter 1. The Battered Hat
paragraphs: Two days after Christmas, I called on my friend Sherlock Holmes. It was a frosty morning, and the windows were thick with ice crystals. Holmes was lying on the sofa in his purple dressing-gown. On the back of a chair beside him hung the shabbiest old hat I had ever seen: black, round and hard, dusty, cracked and stained all over. A magnifying glass lay on the seat.
“Is that hat a clue to some terrible crime?” I asked.
“No, no crime,” laughed Holmes. “Only one of those funny little puzzles that happen when four million people are jostling together in one city. You know Peterson, the commissionaire?”
I did. A commissionaire is a doorman in a smart uniform, and Peterson was a very honest fellow.

“At four o’clock on Christmas morning,” said Holmes, “Peterson was walking home when he saw a tall man carrying a big white goose over his shoulder. Some rough young men started a quarrel with him and knocked off his hat. The man raised his walking stick to defend himself, and, swinging it over his head, he smashed a shop window behind him! Peterson rushed to help. But the man was so shocked at breaking the window, and so alarmed to see somebody in uniform running towards him, that he dropped his goose and ran away. So did the rough young men. Peterson was left with this battered hat and a very fine Christmas goose.

“On the goose’s leg was a card saying ‘For Mrs Henry Baker’, and inside the hat are the letters H. B. But there are hundreds of Henry Bakers in London. So Peterson brought both to me. This morning the goose was starting to need eating, so Peterson has taken it home for his own dinner. I have kept the hat.”
“And what can you tell from an old hat?”
“Here is my magnifying glass, Watson. You know my methods. What can *you* tell about the man who wore it?”
I turned the tattered thing over. “Nothing,” I said.

“On the contrary, Watson, you can see everything. But you do not *reason* from what you see.” Holmes held up the hat. “This man is clever. Three years ago he had plenty of money, but now he has fallen on hard times. He used to be careful, but he is less careful now. Still, he has kept a little pride in himself. He is middle-aged, with greyish hair that was cut a few days ago, and he puts lime-scented cream on it. He does not go out much. He has no gas lights in his house. And I fancy he is not on the best of terms with his wife.”
“Holmes, you must be joking!”

For an answer, Holmes put the hat on his own head. It slid right down over his forehead and stopped on the bridge of his nose. “It is a question of size,” he said, from underneath it. “A man with so large a head must have something in it.

“This was a very expensive hat, but it is three years old; hats with this curly brim were the fashion then. If a man could afford such a hat three years ago and has not bought another since, he has gone down in the world.

“See this little loop? It is for elastic, to stop the hat blowing away. Hats are never sold with them, so he must have asked for one specially: a careful man. But the elastic is broken and he has not mended it, so he is less careful now. Yet he has coloured in the stains with ink to hide them, so he still has some pride.

“Inside the lining are tiny hairs, clean-cut by a barber’s scissors, and they smell of lime cream. The dust is not the gritty grey dust of the street but the fluffy brown dust of a house, so the hat hangs indoors most of the time. There are five spots of candle-wax on the brim. He must often walk upstairs at night with his hat in one hand and a dripping candle in the other. He never got wax on his hat from a gas lamp! And nobody has brushed this hat for weeks. If your wife let you go out looking like that, Watson, I should think you had upset her. That is why he was carrying home a fine goose with her name on it: to make friends again.”
I laughed. “It is very clever,” I said. “But since there has been no crime, it seems rather a waste of your brains.”
At that very moment the door flew open and Peterson burst in, red-cheeked and wide-eyed.
“The goose, Mr Holmes!” he gasped. “The goose, sir!”

chapters.title: Chapter 2. A Jewel in a Goose
paragraphs: “What about it?” said Holmes. “Has it come back to life and flapped off through the kitchen window?”
“See what my wife found inside it!”
In the middle of Peterson’s palm lay a brilliant blue stone, a little smaller than a bean. It twinkled like a star.
Holmes sat up with a whistle. “Peterson! Do you know what you have got?”
“A diamond, sir?”
“It is more than a precious stone. It is *the* precious stone.”
“Not the Countess of Morcar’s blue carbuncle!” I cried.
“Exactly so. Its owner has offered a reward of one thousand pounds to anybody who finds it.”
“A thousand pounds!” Peterson sat down with a bump.

Holmes found the newspaper report. Five days before, the jewel had been stolen from the Countess’s room at the Hotel Cosmopolitan. A plumber called John Horner had been sent up to mend the fireplace. A hotel attendant called James Ryder had shown him up, and had then been called away. When Ryder came back, Horner had gone, and the Countess’s jewel-box lay open and empty. Ryder raised the alarm, and the Countess’s maid, Catherine Cusack, came running. Horner had been in trouble with the police once before. Although he cried out again and again that he was innocent, he had been arrested and was waiting to go on trial.

“So,” said Holmes, “how did a jewel get from a jewel-box in a grand hotel into a goose in Tottenham Court Road? The goose came from Mr Henry Baker, the gentleman with the battered hat. So now we must find him.”

He wrote out an advertisement for the evening newspapers: *Found at the corner of Goodge Street, a goose and a black felt hat. Mr Henry Baker can have the same by calling at 6.30 this evening at 221B Baker Street.*
“Run along, Peterson, and put this in every evening paper,” he said. “And on your way back, buy a goose. We must have one to give this gentleman in place of the one your family is eating.”

When Peterson had gone, Holmes held the stone up to the light. “It’s a bonny thing,” he said. “See how it glints and sparkles. It is not yet twenty years old, yet it has already caused a great deal of trouble. I shall lock it in my strong-box.”
“Do you think Horner the plumber is innocent?”
“I cannot tell yet.”
“And Henry Baker? Was he part of it?”

“I think it much more likely that Henry Baker is perfectly innocent, and had no idea that the bird he was carrying was worth more than if it had been made of solid gold. I shall find out with a very simple test, if he answers our advertisement.”
Clue check: The jewel was stolen from a hotel, but it turned up inside a Christmas goose. How do you think it got there? Who could have put it there?

chapters.title: Chapter 3. A Bet at Covent Garden
paragraphs: At half past six that evening, a tall man in a woolly Scottish bonnet arrived at Baker Street. He had a large head, a clever, kindly face with a pointed grey-brown beard, and a shabby black coat buttoned up to his chin.
“Mr Henry Baker, I believe,” said Holmes. “Is that your hat?”
“Yes, sir, that is certainly my hat.”
“I am afraid we had to eat your goose.”
“Eat it!” Mr Baker half rose from his chair.

“It would have gone bad otherwise. But I hope this goose on the sideboard, which is about the same size and perfectly fresh, will do just as well? Of course, we still have the feathers and the legs and the crop of your own bird, if you would like them.” (A goose’s crop is a little pouch in its throat, where its food goes first.)
Mr Baker laughed heartily. “No, thank you, sir. I shall be quite happy with that excellent bird on your sideboard.”
Holmes glanced at me with a tiny shrug.
“By the way,” he said, “where did you get your goose?”

“At the Alpha Inn, near the British Museum,” said Mr Baker. “The landlord started a goose club. We paid him a few pennies every week, and at Christmas each of us got a goose.” He tucked the new goose under his arm, bowed, and marched off.
“So much for Mr Henry Baker,” said Holmes. “He knows nothing whatever about the jewel. Come, Watson, let us follow this clue while it is still hot.”

It was a bitter night. The stars shone coldly, and our breath puffed out like smoke. At the Alpha Inn, the landlord told us he had bought his geese from a salesman called Breckinridge, at Covent Garden market.

“Remember, Watson,” said Holmes, as we hurried on, “at one end of this chain is a goose, but at the other end is a man who may be sent to prison for years unless we can prove he is innocent. Quick march!”
At Covent Garden, a sharp-faced man with neat side-whiskers was putting up the shutters of a stall marked BRECKINRIDGE.
“Sold out of geese, I see,” said Holmes. “Where did you get the ones you sold to the Alpha?”

To my surprise, the salesman flew into a temper. “I shan’t tell you! Everybody keeps pestering me: ‘Where are the geese? Who did you sell the geese to?’ You’d think they were the only geese in the world!”
“Oh, it doesn’t matter,” said Holmes carelessly. “Only I had a bet that the goose I ate was raised in the country.”
“Then you’ve lost,” snapped the salesman. “It was raised in the town.”
“Nonsense. I’ll bet you a gold sovereign it was country-bred.”

The salesman chuckled. “Bill, bring me the books!” A boy brought out a thin little book and a big greasy one. “Now then, Mr Know-it-all. Here’s the list of the people I buy from. Read out that third name.”
“Mrs Oakshott, 117 Brixton Road,” read Holmes.
“Now look her up in the big book.”
“‘December 22nd. Twenty-four geese.’ And underneath: ‘Sold to Mr Windigate of the Alpha.’”
“What have you got to say now?”
Holmes looked terribly disappointed. He threw a sovereign down on the stall and walked away. But under the next lamp post, he began to shake with silent laughter.

“When you see a man with whiskers like that and a racing newspaper sticking out of his pocket,” he whispered, “you can always get him to talk with a bet. If I had offered him a hundred pounds, he would never have told me so much. And did you notice, Watson? Somebody else is anxious about these geese too.”
Just then a loud noise broke out behind us. A little rat-faced man was standing in the lamplight, and Breckinridge was shaking his fists at him.
“I’ve had enough of you and your geese! Go and ask Mrs Oakshott!”
“She told me to ask you,” whined the little man.
“Then get out!” Breckinridge rushed at him, and the little man fled into the darkness.
“Ha!” whispered Holmes. “Come on!”
Clue check: Holmes said he would test Mr Baker. What was the test? (Think about where the jewel was found.) Why does Mr Baker’s answer show that he knew nothing about it?

chapters.title: Chapter 4. A Blue Egg
paragraphs: Holmes caught up with the little man and touched him on the shoulder. He spun round, and in the gaslight his face was as white as paper.
“Who are you? What do you want?” he quavered.

“My name is Sherlock Holmes. It is my business to know what other people don’t know. You are trying to trace some geese which were sold by Mrs Oakshott of Brixton Road to a salesman called Breckinridge, by him to the Alpha Inn, and by the Alpha to its goose club, of which Mr Henry Baker is a member.”
“Oh, sir, you are the very man I have longed to meet!”
“Then let us talk somewhere warm,” said Holmes, waving down a cab. “But first, whom do I have the pleasure of helping?”
The man hesitated. “My name is John Robinson,” he said, with a sideways look.
“No, no. Your *real* name,” said Holmes sweetly.
The man’s white cheeks turned pink. “James Ryder.”
“Exactly so. Head attendant at the Hotel Cosmopolitan. Step into the cab.”
Nobody spoke on the journey. But I could hear the little man’s quick, nervous breathing, and see him clasping and unclasping his hands.

“Here we are!” said Holmes cheerfully, back at Baker Street. “Take the chair by the fire, Mr Ryder. Now, you want to know what became of those geese? Or rather, I fancy, of one goose: white, with a black bar across its tail.”
Ryder trembled. “Oh, sir, can you tell me where it went?”
“It came here. And a most remarkable bird it was. It laid an egg after it was dead: the bonniest, brightest little blue egg that ever was seen. I have it here in my museum.”
Holmes unlocked his strong-box and held up the blue carbuncle. It shone like a star. Ryder staggered to his feet and clutched the mantelpiece, staring at it.
“The game’s up, Ryder,” said Holmes quietly. “Give him an arm back to his chair, Watson, and a glass of water.”

chapters.title: Chapter 5. Two Geese with Barred Tails
paragraphs: “I already know nearly everything,” said Holmes sternly. “The maid, Catherine Cusack, told you about the Countess’s jewel. You knew that Horner the plumber had been in trouble before, so people would be quick to blame him. You arranged for him to be sent to mend the fireplace. When he had gone, you took the jewel, raised the alarm, and let poor Horner be arrested for something he never did.”
Ryder threw himself down on the rug. “Oh, have mercy, Mr Holmes! Think of my father and mother! I never did anything wrong before, and I never will again!”
“Get back in your chair,” said Holmes. “It is all very well to be sorry now. But you did not think much about poor Horner, waiting in prison. Now tell us: how did the stone get into the goose?”

Ryder licked his dry lips. “I was afraid the police might search me at any moment,” he said. “So I hurried to my sister’s house in Brixton Road. She is Mrs Oakshott, and she fattens geese for the market. I wanted to take the stone to a friend of mine in Kilburn, who knew how to sell stolen things. But how could I carry it there safely? Then I looked down at the geese waddling round my feet, and I had an idea that would beat the best detective that ever lived.

“My sister had promised me a goose for Christmas. So I caught one, a big white one with a barred tail, and I pushed the stone right down its throat. The bird gave a gulp, and I felt the stone slide down into its crop. But the goose flapped and struggled, and my sister came out to see what was the matter. As I turned to speak to her, the bird broke free and ran off among the others.
“‘Whatever are you doing with that bird, Jem?’ she said.

“‘You said you’d give me one for Christmas,’ I told her, ‘and I was feeling which was the fattest. If it’s all the same to you, Maggie, I’d like the white one with the barred tail, in the middle of the flock.’
“‘Oh, very well,’ she said, a little huffy. ‘Take it with you.’

“So I carried that goose all the way to Kilburn. But when my friend and I looked inside it, there was no stone! My heart turned to water. I rushed back to my sister’s, and there was not a single bird left in the yard.
“‘Where are they all, Maggie?’ I cried.
“‘Gone to Breckinridge, the dealer at Covent Garden.’
“‘But was there another goose with a barred tail, the same as mine?’
“‘Yes, Jem, there were two barred-tailed ones, and I could never tell them apart.’

“Then I saw it all. I ran to Breckinridge, but he had sold the lot, and he would not tell me where they had gone. And now I am a thief, and I never even got to keep the jewel!” He buried his face in his hands and sobbed.
For a long time there was silence, except for the tap, tap, tap of Holmes’s fingertips on the table. Then my friend stood up and threw open the door.
“Get out!” he said.
“What, sir? Oh, bless you!”
“No more words. Get out!”
There was a rush, a clatter on the stairs, the bang of a door, and the sound of running feet fading away down the street.

“After all, Watson,” said Holmes, settling back in his chair, “I am not paid by the police to do their work for them. Ryder will not dare to speak against Horner now, so the case against Horner will fall to pieces, and he will go free. Ryder will not do wrong again; he is far too frightened. If I sent him to prison now, I might make him a criminal for life. Besides, it is the season of forgiveness. The Countess shall have her jewel back, and chance has given us a most curious puzzle. Solving it is its own reward.”
He rubbed his hands together.
“And now, Doctor, if you would ring the bell, we will begin another investigation, in which a bird will also be the main feature. I believe Mrs Hudson is roasting a woodcock for our supper.”
